data.raw_text:
The “Grand Bargain” Revisited
- Northern Shade

“I did it for my country…”
The echo still reverberates. Some scoff, but the general populace winces.

Here’s what many refuse to see: the fracture isn’t merely between Manila and Mindanao (though it exists), nor just between elites and masses. It runs deeper, between those who still believe in the Filipino capacity to reckon with our own, and those who prefer judgment outsourced to others.

The elites in their ivory towers and air-conditioned conscience, sipping imported ideals, see Duterte as a monster to be paraded before foreign courts. But for the Visayas, for Mindanao (80-90%), for the heartland, whose lives were reshaped by order, however harsh, he remains present, not past, not memory, but a living ledger of what we demanded and what we allowed.

This is not nostalgia. It is the residue of the “grand bargain” Manolo Quezon once described: Duterte vowed to wield the blade, to cut through rot, crime, and decay, and we stood by him. (Inspired by article)

“I’ll take the hits. Hang me if you must,” he said.
And he did, imperfectly, sometimes brutally, but he did so as our President, and importantly with our consent.

His approval soared to nearly 90% by term’s end not because people were blind, but because they saw a man willing to absorb the cost of action when others only spoke of reform. The bargain was simple: he would take the blows/take all the blame, and we would guard the fire he lit.

“I did it for my COUNTRY…”

Those words now echo again, not in unity but in challenge. Because the guard has changed. The light is dimming. The control is shifting.

The current administration, once bold on this issue, now hides behind process and pretense. They know an undercurrent (among several) simmers, that the safety people once felt under that bargain has soured into grief, and grief into anger. We were not allowed to handle our reckoning, it was taken from us, replaced by foreign judges and borrowed moralities. And they did it with undisguised glee.

Yes, there were excesses, lives lost, lines crossed, consciences unsettled. But the point is this, we knew, and we allowed it. That is our burden and our right. The reckoning for those choices belongs to US alone, not to The HAGUE, not to anyone else.

He shielded us, clumsily, loudly, sometimes cruelly, but he did so as our President. In a world that discards its own and bows to outsiders, we still owe him that recognition, not sainthood, but ownership. He was ours, HE was us, and He is one of us.

“I would rather have a country run like hell by Filipinos than a country run like heaven by the Americans.”
— Manuel L. Quezon

It’s time to MEAN the second part.

"Because however bad a Filipino government might be, WE can always change it."
